summary.text: The proof’s core is a tail-mass transformation: tail sums satisfy an integer-averaging flow recurrence, and monotone staircase deficits show that stabilization occurs exactly when the penultimate tail first reaches \(1\). Comparing source masses \(N\) and \(N+1\), the pointwise flow difference is a \(0\)-\(1\) prefix whose unit increment propagates along the already saturated diagonal, forcing the new hitting time to be at most two steps later, while finite-speed propagation makes it strictly later than the old one.

full_proof.text:
Let the sites be indexed by the nonnegative integers, from left to right. All divisions below are integer divisions, so \(x/2=\lfloor x/2\rfloor\).

We prove the result by replacing the individual cell masses by tail sums. This turns the cellular-automaton rule into a particularly simple averaging recurrence.

Define \(F_N(t,j)\), for \(N,t,j\geq 0\), by
\[
 F_N(0,0)=N,\qquad F_N(0,j)=0\quad(j>0),
\]
\[
 F_N(t,0)=N\quad(t>0),
\]
and
\[
 F_N(t+1,j+1)=\left\lfloor\frac{F_N(t,j)+F_N(t,j+1)}2\right\rfloor.
 \tag{1}
\]
Later we will show that \(F_N(t,j)\) is exactly the total mass at sites \(j,j+1,\ldots\) after \(t\) cellular-automaton steps.

For positive \(N\), define the hitting time
\[
 b(N)=\min\{t:F_N(t,N-1)=1\}.
 \tag{2}
\]
We will prove first that this set is nonempty and that
\[
 b(N)<b(N+1)\leq b(N)+2. \tag{3}
\]
Since all quantities are integers, (3) says precisely that
\[
 b(N+1)=b(N)+1\quad\hbox{or}\quad b(N+1)=b(N)+2.
 \tag{4}
\]
Finally we identify \(b(N)\) with the stabilization time \(a(N)\) of the original automaton.


1. Staircase bounds and deficits
--------------------------------

The fundamental bound is
\[
 0\leq F_N(t,j)\leq N-j, \tag{5}
\]
where the right side is understood as truncated subtraction and hence is zero when \(j\geq N\).

To prove the upper bound, induct on \(t\). At time zero it is immediate: the value is \(N\) at site 0 and zero elsewhere. At site 0 the bound remains an equality at every time. For a site \(j+1\), suppose
\[
 F_N(t,j)\leq N-j,\qquad F_N(t,j+1)\leq N-(j+1).
\]
The sum of these two staircase bounds is at most twice \(N-(j+1)\), plus at most one. Dividing by 2 and taking the floor therefore gives
\[
 F_N(t+1,j+1)\leq N-(j+1).
\]
This proves (5). In particular, \(F_N(t,j)=0\) for every \(j\geq N\).

The profile is also nonincreasing in the spatial variable:
\[
 F_N(t,j+1)\leq F_N(t,j). \tag{6}
\]
This follows by induction on time. At time zero it is clear. For positive sites, (1) and the induction hypothesis compare the two parent sums term by term. At the left boundary, the value at site 0 is \(N\), while the staircase bound already gives that every other value is at most \(N\).

It follows that the flow is nondecreasing in time at each fixed site:
\[
 F_N(t,j)\leq F_N(t+1,j). \tag{7}
\]
For \(j=0\) this is equality. For \(j=k+1\), (6) gives \(F_N(t,k)\geq F_N(t,k+1)\), and hence
\[
 \left\lfloor\frac{F_N(t,k)+F_N(t,k+1)}2\right\rfloor
 \geq F_N(t,k+1).
\]

Introduce the deficit below the staircase:
\[
 H_N(t,j)=N-j-F_N(t,j). \tag{8}
\]
By (5), this is a nonnegative integer. A direct substitution in (1), taking account of the parity of two consecutive staircase values, gives the important recurrence
\[
 H_N(t+1,j+1)
 =\left\lfloor\frac{H_N(t,j)+H_N(t,j+1)}2\right\rfloor.
 \tag{9}
\]
Indeed, the parent staircase values are \(N-j\) and \(N-j-1\), whose sum is odd; subtracting the floor of the corresponding flow average from the child staircase value \(N-j-1\) yields exactly the floor of the average of the two deficits. Also
\[
 H_N(t,0)=0 \tag{10}
\]
for all \(t\). By (7), deficits are nonincreasing in time:
\[
 H_N(t+1,j)\leq H_N(t,j). \tag{11}
\]
Thus, once a deficit becomes zero, it remains zero.

Every deficit eventually becomes zero. We prove this by induction on the site \(j\). Site 0 is already clear by (10). Suppose site \(j\) is clear at some time \(t\), and let the deficit at site \(j+1\) then be \(v\). If \(v=0\), there is nothing to prove. If \(v>0\), then at the next time site \(j\) remains clear and (9) changes the right deficit from \(v\) to \(\lfloor v/2\rfloor<v\). Repeating this argument, or formally inducting on \(v\), eventually reduces the right deficit to zero. This proves eventual clearing at every site.

Consequently we may define the first clearing time
\[
 \tau_N(j)=\min\{t:H_N(t,j)=0\}. \tag{12}
\]
The minimum exists by the preceding paragraph. By definition,
\[
 H_N(\tau_N(j),j)=0, \tag{13}
\]
and if \(t<\tau_N(j)\), then \(H_N(t,j)>0\).

Inside the staircase, clearing advances by at least one time step per site:
\[
 \tau_N(j)+1\leq \tau_N(j+1)\qquad\text{if }j+1<N. \tag{14}
\]
To see this, write \(\tau_N(j+1)=s+1\). It cannot be zero, because initially the deficit at every site \(j+1<N\) is \(N-(j+1)>0\). Just before clearing, the right deficit \(H_N(s,j+1)\) is positive, while at time \(s+1\) it is zero. By (9),
\[
 \left\lfloor\frac{H_N(s,j)+H_N(s,j+1)}2\right\rfloor=0.
\]
The sum of the two nonnegative deficits is therefore less than 2. Since the second is positive, it equals 1 and the first must equal 0. Thus site \(j\) has cleared by time \(s\), so \(\tau_N(j)\leq s\), proving (14).

Iterating (14), whenever \(j+d<N\), gives
\[
 \tau_N(j)+d\leq \tau_N(j+d). \tag{15}
\]

At the target site \(N-1\), the staircase value is 1. Hence, for \(N\geq1\),
\[
 H_N(t,N-1)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad F_N(t,N-1)=1. \tag{16}
\]
It follows both that the hitting set in (2) is nonempty and that
\[
 b(N)=\tau_N(N-1). \tag{17}
\]
For reference, the smallest cases are \(b(1)=0\) and \(b(2)=1\).


2. Comparing source masses \(N\) and \(N+1\)
------------------------------------------------

Define the source-difference field
\[
 D_N(t,j)=F_{N+1}(t,j)-F_N(t,j). \tag{18}
\]
The flow is monotone in its source mass, as follows immediately by induction from (1), so this difference is nonnegative. More strongly,
\[
 D_N(t,j)\in\{0,1\}. \tag{19}
\]
Indeed, at time zero this is clear: the difference is 1 at site 0 and 0 elsewhere. Suppose it is true for the two parents of a site. Write their smaller-flow values as \(x,y\), and their differences as \(\delta,\epsilon\in\{0,1\}\). Then the child difference is
\[
 \left\lfloor\frac{x+y+\delta+\epsilon}{2}\right\rfloor
 -\left\lfloor\frac{x+y}{2}\right\rfloor.
\]
Because \(0\leq\delta+\epsilon\leq2\), this difference is either 0 or 1. This proves (19). We will use in particular
\[
 F_{N+1}(t,j)=F_N(t,j)+D_N(t,j). \tag{20}
\]

We next need a diagonal propagation fact. Suppose \(k+1<N\), both sites \(k,k+1\) are saturated for the smaller flow,
\[
 H_N(t,k)=H_N(t,k+1)=0,
\]
and \(D_N(t,k)=1\). Then
\[
 D_N(t+1,k+1)=1. \tag{21}
\]
To verify this, saturation says
\[
 F_N(t,k)=N-k,
 \qquad F_N(t,k+1)=N-k-1.
\]
If \(D_N(t,k+1)=1\), both parent values for the larger source exceed the smaller ones by 1, so their sum exceeds it by 2 and the child floor-average exceeds it by 1. If instead \(D_N(t,k+1)=0\), the larger parent sum exceeds the smaller one by exactly 1. But the smaller parent sum
\[
 (N-k)+(N-k-1)=2(N-k)-1
\]
is odd. Adding 1 therefore raises its floor-half by exactly 1. This proves (21) in both cases.

Let
\[
 T=\tau_N(N-1)=b(N),

given \(N\geq2\). We claim
\[
 D_N(T,N-2)=1. \tag{22}
\]
Consider the diagonal points
\[
 \bigl(T-(N-2)+k,\,k\bigr),\qquad 0\leq k\leq N-2.
 \tag{23}
\]
The initial time in (23) is nonnegative: from (15), applied from site 0 to site \(N-1\), and \(\tau_N(0)=0\), we have \(T\geq N-1\).

At \(k=0\), the difference is 1 because both flows retain their source values at site 0. Suppose the difference is 1 at the point corresponding to \(k\). At its time, both sites \(k\) and \(k+1\) have already cleared. Indeed, (15), applied from either of these sites to \(N-1\), bounds its clearing time by the time displayed in (23). Therefore both deficits there are zero. The propagation rule (21) now shows that the difference is 1 at the next diagonal point. Induction up to \(k=N-2\) proves (22).

We can now establish the upper bound in (3). Again let \(T=b(N)\), first assuming \(N\geq2\). By (15), site \(N-2\) is clear by time \(T\), so
\[
 F_N(T,N-2)=2.

given (22) and (20),
\[
 F_{N+1}(T,N-2)=3. \tag{24}
\]
Also the old target is clear, so
\[
 F_N(T,N-1)=1,

given source monotonicity,
\[
 F_{N+1}(T,N-1)\geq1. \tag{25}
\]
At the next time, (1), (24), and (25) give
\[
 F_{N+1}(T+1,N-1)
 =\left\lfloor\frac{F_{N+1}(T,N-2)+F_{N+1}(T,N-1)}2\right\rfloor
 \geq2. \tag{26}
\]
At site \(N\), the value at time \(T+1\) is nonnegative. Applying (1) once more to (26) therefore gives
\[
 F_{N+1}(T+2,N)\geq1. \tag{27}
\]
But the staircase bound for source \(N+1\) at site \(N\) is exactly 1, so equality holds in (27). Site \(N\) is the new target; hence
\[
 b(N+1)\leq T+2=b(N)+2. \tag{28}
\]
For \(N=1\), this same conclusion follows directly from \(b(1)=0\), \(b(2)=1\).

It remains to prove strict growth. For \(N\geq2\), we show the stronger assertion
\[
 F_{N+1}(s,N)=0\qquad(0\leq s\leq T), \tag{29}
\]
where \(T=b(N)=\tau_N(N-1)\). We induct on \(s\). At time zero it is clear. Suppose \(s+1\leq T\) and (29) holds at time \(s\). Since \(s<T\), the old target deficit has not cleared. Its staircase bound is 1, so its flow value must be 0:
\[
 F_N(s,N-1)=0. \tag{30}
\]
By (19) and (20),
\[
 F_{N+1}(s,N-1)\leq1. \tag{31}
\]
The other parent of the new target is \(F_{N+1}(s,N)=0\) by induction. Thus (1) and (31) show
\[
 F_{N+1}(s+1,N)=\left\lfloor\frac{F_{N+1}(s,N-1)+0}{2}\right\rfloor=0.
\]
This proves (29).

If the new hitting time were at most \(T\), monotonicity in time would give
\[
 1=F_{N+1}(b(N+1),N)\leq F_{N+1}(T,N)=0,
\]
a contradiction. Therefore
\[
 b(N)<b(N+1). \tag{32}
\]
For \(N=1\), this is again the direct calculation \(b(1)=0<b(2)=1\).

Combining (28) and (32), the integer \(b(N+1)\) lies strictly above \(b(N)\) and no higher than \(b(N)+2\). This proves (4).


3. Identification with the cellular automaton
----------------------------------------------

We now connect the scalar flow to the sequence in the question.

For a finite mass configuration \(L=(m_0,m_1,\ldots)\), define its tail sum
\[
 Q_L(j)=\sum_{i\geq j}m_i,
\]
where entries beyond the finite list are zero. Removing trailing zero entries does not change any tail sum.

In one untrimmed automaton step, a cell of mass \(m\) keeps
\[
 \left\lceil\frac m2\right\rceil=\left\lfloor\frac{m+1}{2}\right\rfloor

given sends
\[
 \left\lfloor\frac m2\right\rfloor

to its right neighbor. These two quantities sum to \(m\).

Let \(L'\) be the result after one step, with or without deletion of trailing zeros. Conservation of total mass gives
\[
 Q_{L'}(0)=Q_L(0). \tag{33}
\]
For \(j\geq0\), a direct summation of the updated cells from site \(j+1\) onward gives
\[
 Q_{L'}(j+1)
 =\left\lfloor\frac{Q_L(j)+Q_L(j+1)}2\right\rfloor. \tag{34}
\]
For completeness, write the mass at site \(j\) as
\(m_j=Q_L(j)-Q_L(j+1)\). The mass entering the tail beginning at \(j+1\) from site \(j\) is \(\lfloor m_j/2\rfloor\), while all mass already strictly to the right is redistributed internally and remains in that tail. Equivalently, summing the kept and received halves cell by cell and using \(\lceil m/2\rceil+\lfloor m/2\rfloor=m\) yields (34). The parity identity implicit here is
\[
 Q_L(j+1)+\left\lfloor\frac{Q_L(j)-Q_L(j+1)}2\right\rfloor
 =\left\lfloor\frac{Q_L(j)+Q_L(j+1)}2\right\rfloor.
\]

Initially the configuration is \([N]\), whose tail sums are \(N\) at site 0 and 0 at every positive site. Equations (33) and (34) are exactly the defining recurrence (1). Therefore, by induction on time,
\[
 Q_{S_N(t)}(j)=F_N(t,j) \tag{35}
\]
for every \(t,j\), where \(S_N(t)\) is the actual cellular-automaton configuration after \(t\) trimmed steps.

We must show that reaching the stable list of \(N\) ones is equivalent to the scalar target hit.

If
\[
 S_N(t)=(1,1,\ldots,1)

given \(N\) entries, then its tail from site \(N-1\) has sum 1. By (35),
\[
 F_N(t,N-1)=1. \tag{36}
\]

Conversely, suppose \(F_N(t,N-1)=1\). By (16), the target deficit has cleared by time \(t\). For any \(j<N\), (15) gives
\[
 \tau_N(j)+(N-1-j)\leq\tau_N(N-1)\leq t.
\]
In particular \(\tau_N(j)\leq t\), so site \(j\)'s deficit is zero and
\[
 F_N(t,j)=N-j. \tag{37}
\]
For \(j\geq N\), the staircase bound gives \(F_N(t,j)=0=N-j\). Thus (37) holds for every \(j\geq0\).

Using (35), every tail sum of the actual configuration is therefore \(N-j\). Successive differences of tail sums show that every occupied entry has mass 1: the mass at site \(j\) is
\[
 Q_{S_N(t)}(j)-Q_{S_N(t)}(j+1)
 =(N-j)-(N-j-1)=1

given \(j<N\), and it is zero thereafter. Because the automaton removes all trailing zeros after every step (and the initial positive list has none), the represented finite list has no trailing zero. Hence it is exactly the list of \(N\) ones. We have proved
\[
 S_N(t)=(1,\ldots,1)
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 F_N(t,N-1)=1. \tag{38}
\]

The stabilization time \(a(N)\) is the least \(t\) satisfying the left side of (38), while \(b(N)\) is the least \(t\) satisfying the right side. Therefore
\[
 a(N)=b(N)\qquad(N\geq1). \tag{39}
\]

Applying (4) and then (39), for every \(N\geq1\),
\[
 a(N+1)=a(N)+1
 \quad\text{or}\quad
 a(N+1)=a(N)+2.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
 a(N+1)-a(N)\in\{1,2\}.
\]
This is the desired statement.
